output.title: Shared logins hide a workflow cost you only notice later
output.body:
Shared logins are usually a convenience choice, not a strategy. For an owner-run small business, the hidden cost is not abstract: you lose the clean record of who changed what, who still has access, and who handed the password to the next person. That turns a simple account into a small audit problem.

The workarounds are familiar. Someone keeps a password note, a spreadsheet, or becomes the human router for every account. It keeps things moving, but only just.

The practical next step is simple: ask, “Who has access to our shared accounts, who gave it to them, and when should that access end?” If nobody can answer that cleanly, you have found the gap. Treat that as a workflow decision, not a technology one.

Then do one manual pass: list the shared accounts, note who actually needs each one, and write down the owner for each access grant. Once the access record exists, you can decide whether the right fix is a password manager, role-based access, or leaving it manual for now.

Shared logins work until they don’t. That is usually when the missing record shows up.
